title: The Ruined Man Who Became Rich Again Through a Dream

keywords: the ruined man who became rich again through a dream
full_text:
There was once in Baghdad a wealthy merchant who, through shipwrecks and misfortune, lost his entire fortune. Reduced to absolute poverty, he had to sell his furniture, his carpets, and his books, retaining only his small ancestral house with its overgrown courtyard garden.

One night, exhausted from a day of vain search for labor, he fell asleep with a heavy heart. In a dream, a venerable figure clothed in green appeared to him and said: 'Rise, O traveler! Your fortune awaits you in the city of Cairo; journey thither, and you shall find abundance!'

Believing the vision, the merchant packed a dry crust of bread, took his walking staff, and set forth on foot across the scorching Syrian desert and the Sinai. After weeks of exhausting travel and blistered feet, he arrived in Cairo, penniless and in rags.

Having no money for lodging, he took refuge in the courtyard of a neighborhood mosque to spend the night.

That very night, a band of thieves broke into the house adjacent to the mosque. The neighbors raised an outcry, and the Chief of Police rushed to the scene with his night watchmen. Finding the mosque empty save for the strange traveler sleeping upon the stones, the police seized him, assumed he was an accomplice, and gave him twenty lashes with a palm-cudgel before throwing him into a cell.

The next morning, the police captain questioned him: 'Who are you, and what brought you to Cairo?'

The merchant weeping recounted his dream: 'I was a wealthy merchant of Baghdad. A dream commanded me to travel to Cairo to find my fortune. I walked across deserts, only to find twenty lashes and an iron chain!'

The captain laughed uproariously, slapping his knee: 'O foolish man of little wit! Three times have I dreamed that in the city of Baghdad, in a quiet quarter, behind an old house with an overgrown courtyard, beneath an ancient fig tree beside a sun-dial, a great treasure of gold dinars is buried! Yet do you see me running to Baghdad on the word of a dream? Go back to your city, you credulous fool, and here are two dinars to buy bread for your journey!'

The merchant took the two dinars, smiled through his tears, and walked back to Baghdad. Arriving at his own house, he took a spade, went into his overgrown courtyard, and dug beneath the ancient fig tree beside the sundial. There he unearthed a brass chest filled with gold dinars and jewels, enough to restore his family to wealth for seven generations, thanking the heavens that a journey to Cairo was necessary to teach him to dig in his own garden.
moral: The treasure you seek across distant lands is often buried in your own home, waiting for patient eyes to see.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
